title: V'Zot HaBerachah: from the mountain (Deuteronomy 34:1–4)
hookLine: from Mount Nebo Moses sees the land he won't enter
tomorrow: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)

lines: A PLACE YOU MAY NEVER STAND.
cards: Grandparents plant trees their grandchildren will sit under. Founders start things they'll have to hand on.
A child fully grown, a cause won, a garden that will only be beautiful in thirty years: most people carry at least one goal they may not live to see finished.
It's one of the strangest human habits, working hard toward a place you may never stand in. Moses spent forty years walking toward a land. Today he gets to see it.

teach.h: UP TO NEBO, TO THE TOP OF PISGAH.
teach.b: Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, across from Jericho.

teach.h: FROM DAN TO THE WESTERN SEA.
teach.b: And God shows him the land: Gilead as far as Dan, the lands of the tribes, the hill country, the plain, all the way to the western sea, and the Negev in the south.

Then God says: "This is the land which I swore unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying: I will give it unto thy seed; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither."
He sees all of it. He will not enter.

Earlier, in Va'etchanan, Moses had pleaded to be allowed across. A midrash counts his pleading as five hundred fifteen prayers, the number value of the Hebrew word va'etchanan, and I pleaded. The answer was still no.
And yet here he climbs anyway. The text records no complaint at the top. Only seeing.
Some commentators read the view as a gift. Rashi says God showed Moses not just the land but its future, what would happen there to his people for generations. Others read it simply.
He saw the place he'd led everyone toward, and the text lets that be enough.
A mountain traditionally identified as Nebo still stands in Jordan today, looking west. The Torah doesn't hide the cost. He doesn't arrive.

how: The final chapter of Deuteronomy, with Moses on Mount Nebo, is read on Simchat Torah; in many communities its closing verses are read with special honor as the end of the yearly Torah cycle.

o: and these are the journeys: the wilderness stops
and this is the land: the view from the hilltop
and this is the blessing: the Torah's final portion

games.q: on the mountain — tap the pairs.
p: the midrash's count of his pleas

s: Moses enters the promised land at the very end
he sees it all and is not allowed to cross.
a midrash counts Moses' pleading as 515 prayers

games.q: you've been told you won't enter the land. God invites you up the mountain to look at it. what does Moses do?
games.why: he climbs Nebo and sees from Dan to the western sea, the whole land he led them toward.

practice: Name one thing you're working toward that might take longer than your life, a family healed, a town changed, a world a little fairer.
Picture yourself on a hilltop, looking at it from a distance; you don't have to be standing in it to care about it, and for now, the seeing can be enough.

wordCard.voice: V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. And in it, the view from Nebo: the land Moses sees, and won't enter.
